To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The Mathematician Ridge is a 2-km-wide and 1-km-deep linear feature that extends for more than 200 km along the equator of the Pacific Ocean.
Mathematician Ridge, the Clipperton Ridge and the East Pacific Rise system are all part of the same ridge system and that the Clipperton and East Pacific Ridges are the same feature.

1) the Clipperton Ridge is a topographic ridge that has been active in the past 10 Ma, 2) the Clippertont Ridge is the result of an upwelling of mantle material, 3) the Clippeton Ridge is a topography feature that has not been formed as a result of a plate tectonically process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the application of the depth–age correlation technique to the Clipperton Ridge and the Mathematician Ridge.
the topography and bathymetry of a region of the East Pacific Rise between the equator and the Clipperton Fracture Zone (Fig. 2).
the interpretation of the topography of the East Pacific Rise system in relation to the generation and evolution of oceanic crust.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the East Pacific Rise is a seafloor-spreading system which has been active since about 10 Ma.
the age of the seafloor in this region is 1–5 m.y. old, with the exception of the Galapagos Rise (Fig.1).
the East Pacific Rise system is a seafloor-spreading system, that the rate of seafloor generation is 4 cm year−1 and that the system was initiated about 3 million years ago.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the East Pacific Rise between the equator and 20° N is older than 10 million years (Ma) and between 0 and 20°S it is younger.
the crust generated at the equator is about 2 m.y. younger than crust generated at 20° S and 20° N, and that the age of the equatorial crust decreases northwards and southwards from 0°.
the crust of the equatorial East Pacific Rise is about 10 m.y. old, which is consistent with its age as determined from magnetic anomaly studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ridge is a topographic expression of an underlying tectonic boundary, and it is a topographic feature that is not a result of volcanism alone, said lead author and geologist David Graham, of the University of Texas at Austin.
the Clipperton Fracture Zone, a 1,000-mile-long fault that runs through the Pacific Ocean, has a much more complicated history than previously thought.
the Earth’s magnetic field has been much stronger over most of its history, with a peak at about 3 billion years ago, when the field strength may have been 60 times stronger than today.
